CHAPTER 35 - PLANE

Introduction

A plane is a flat, two-dimensional surface that extends without limit in every direction. A tabletop, a wall or a sheet of paper suggests part of a plane, but a true plane has no edges and no thickness. In three-dimensional coordinate geometry we describe such a surface by an algebraic equation connecting the coordinates x, y and z of every point that lies on it. This chapter develops the equation of a plane in its various forms, shows how to switch between them, and uses them to answer geometric questions: the angle between two planes, the perpendicular distance of a point from a plane, when two planes are parallel or perpendicular, and how to describe a plane that passes through the line of intersection of two given planes. The single idea that ties everything together is the NORMAL to the plane - a direction perpendicular to the surface. Once the normal is known, almost every property of the plane follows.

35.1 GENERAL EQUATION OF A PLANE

The most general first-degree (linear) equation in x, y and z is

   Ax + By + Cz + D = 0

where A, B, C are not all zero. Every such equation represents a plane, and conversely every plane has an equation of this form. The key fact is that the coefficients of x, y and z form the NORMAL VECTOR to the plane: n = (A, B, C). Any two points P and Q on the plane give a vector PQ that lies IN the plane, and one can show that (A, B, C) is perpendicular to every such in-plane vector. So the triple (A, B, C) fixes the ORIENTATION (tilt) of the plane, while the constant D fixes its POSITION (how far it is shifted from the origin). If D = 0 the plane passes through the origin, because (0, 0, 0) then satisfies the equation. Special cases are worth remembering: z = 0 is the xy-plane, y = 0 is the zx-plane, x = 0 is the yz-plane; x = k is a plane parallel to the yz-plane at distance k; and so on.

35.2 NORMAL FORM OF A PLANE

Suppose we draw the perpendicular ON from the origin O to the plane, meeting it at N, and let this perpendicular have length p (a positive number). Let (l, m, n) be the DIRECTION COSINES of ON, so that l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1. Then a point R with position coordinates (x, y, z) lies on the plane exactly when the projection of OR on the direction ON equals p. This gives the NORMAL FORM

   lx + my + nz = p

Here p is the perpendicular distance of the plane from the origin, and (l, m, n) are the direction cosines of that perpendicular. To convert the general equation Ax + By + Cz + D = 0 into normal form, divide throughout by sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + C^2) and arrange the sign so that the right-hand side is positive:

   (A x + B y + C z)/sqrt(A^2+B^2+C^2) = -D/sqrt(A^2+B^2+C^2)

The coefficients of x, y, z on the left are then the direction cosines l, m, n and the right side is p. For example, for 2x - 2y + z = 12 we have sqrt(4+4+1) = 3, so the normal form is (2/3)x - (2/3)y + (1/3)z = 4; the direction cosines of the normal are (2/3, -2/3, 1/3) and the distance from the origin is p = 4.

35.3 EQUATION OF A PLANE THROUGH A GIVEN POINT WITH A GIVEN NORMAL

A plane is completely determined once we know ONE point on it and a direction normal to it. Let the point be P(x1, y1, z1) and let the normal direction be n = (A, B, C). If R(x, y, z) is any point of the plane, the vector PR = (x - x1, y - y1, z - z1) lies in the plane and so is perpendicular to n. Setting their dot product to zero gives the CARTESIAN form

   A(x - x1) + B(y - y1) + C(z - z1) = 0

Expanding, this is Ax + By + Cz + D = 0 with D = -(A x1 + B y1 + C z1), confirming that the coefficients of x, y, z are again the normal components. In VECTOR notation, if a is the position vector of P and n is the normal, the condition (r - a) . n = 0 becomes

   r . n = a . n

For instance, the plane through (2, 3, -1) with normal (4, 5, 6) is 4(x-2) + 5(y-3) + 6(z+1) = 0, i.e. 4x + 5y + 6z - 17 = 0. This point-normal idea is the workhorse of the whole chapter.

35.4 INTERCEPT FORM OF A PLANE

Suppose a plane cuts the x-axis at (a, 0, 0), the y-axis at (0, b, 0) and the z-axis at (0, 0, c); the numbers a, b, c are the INTERCEPTS the plane makes on the three axes. Substituting these three points into the general equation and eliminating the coefficients leads to the elegant INTERCEPT FORM

   x/a + y/b + z/c = 1

This form is handy when the intercepts are known or wanted. To find the intercepts of a plane given in general form, rewrite it with the constant on the right and divide through. For example, 2x + 3y + 4z = 12 becomes x/6 + y/4 + z/3 = 1, so the intercepts are 6, 4 and 3 on the x, y and z axes respectively. A plane parallel to an axis makes no (infinite) intercept on it, so that variable is absent from the equation.

35.5 PLANE PASSING THROUGH THREE GIVEN POINTS

Three points that are not collinear determine a unique plane. If the points are P1(x1, y1, z1), P2(x2, y2, z2) and P3(x3, y3, z3), the equation of the plane can be written as the determinant

   | x - x1   y - y1   z - z1 |
   | x2 - x1  y2 - y1  z2 - z1 | = 0
   | x3 - x1  y3 - y1  z3 - z1 |

The first row is the vector from P1 to the general point R; the other two rows are the vectors P1P2 and P1P3, which lie in the plane. The determinant vanishing expresses that these three vectors are coplanar. Equivalently, one may compute the normal as the cross product P1P2 x P1P3 and then use the point-normal form. For example, for the points (1, 1, 1), (1, 2, 3) and (2, -1, 1), P1P2 = (0, 1, 2) and P1P3 = (1, -2, 0); their cross product is (4, 2, -1), so the plane is 4(x-1) + 2(y-1) - (z-1) = 0, i.e. 4x + 2y - z = 5.

35.6 VECTOR EQUATION OF A PLANE

Vectors give the cleanest description of a plane. Let n be a vector normal to the plane and let a be the position vector of a fixed point on it. A point with position vector r lies on the plane when (r - a) is perpendicular to n, i.e.

   r . n = a . n = d

where d = a . n is a constant. This is the vector equation of the plane in the form r . n = d. If we use the UNIT normal n_hat (so |n_hat| = 1), the equation becomes r . n_hat = p, which is the vector form of the normal form; p is again the perpendicular distance from the origin. Writing r = x i + y j + z k and n = A i + B j + C k recovers the Cartesian equation Ax + By + Cz = d. Thus r . n = d and Ax + By + Cz = d are the same statement in two languages. The vector equation of a plane through three points a, b, c can be written r . [(b - a) x (c - a)] = a . [(b - a) x (c - a)], using the cross product to build the normal.

35.7 ANGLE BETWEEN TWO PLANES

The angle between two planes is defined as the angle between their normals. If the planes are A1x + B1y + C1z + D1 = 0 and A2x + B2y + C2z + D2 = 0, with normals n1 = (A1, B1, C1) and n2 = (A2, B2, C2), then the angle theta between them satisfies

   cos theta = |A1 A2 + B1 B2 + C1 C2| / [ sqrt(A1^2+B1^2+C1^2) sqrt(A2^2+B2^2+C2^2) ]

The modulus is taken so that theta is the acute angle between the planes. In vector form, cos theta = |n1 . n2| / (|n1| |n2|). Two important special cases follow at once. The planes are PARALLEL when their normals are parallel, i.e.

   A1/A2 = B1/B2 = C1/C2

(the coefficients are proportional). The planes are PERPENDICULAR when their normals are perpendicular, i.e. the dot product of the normals is zero:

   A1 A2 + B1 B2 + C1 C2 = 0

For example, the angle between x + 2y + 2z = 5 and 2x - y + 2z = 3 uses n1 . n2 = (1)(2)+(2)(-1)+(2)(2) = 4, |n1| = 3, |n2| = 3, so cos theta = 4/9 and theta = cos^-1(4/9), about 63.6 degrees.

35.8 DISTANCE OF A POINT FROM A PLANE

The perpendicular distance of a point P(x1, y1, z1) from the plane Ax + By + Cz + D = 0 is

   d = |A x1 + B y1 + C z1 + D| / sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + C^2)

The numerator is the value obtained by substituting the point into the left side of the equation; the denominator is the length of the normal vector. The modulus makes the distance positive. If the point is the origin, the distance reduces to |D|/sqrt(A^2+B^2+C^2), matching the p of the normal form. As a worked example, the distance of (1, 2, 3) from 2x - y + 2z + 3 = 0 is |2(1) - 2 + 2(3) + 3| / sqrt(4+1+4) = |9|/3 = 3. The DISTANCE BETWEEN TWO PARALLEL planes Ax + By + Cz + D1 = 0 and Ax + By + Cz + D2 = 0 (same normal) is |D1 - D2|/sqrt(A^2+B^2+C^2).

35.9 PLANE THROUGH THE INTERSECTION OF TWO PLANES

Two non-parallel planes meet in a straight line. Any plane that contains this line of intersection can be written, using a parameter lambda, as

   (A1x + B1y + C1z + D1) + lambda (A2x + B2y + C2z + D2) = 0

For every value of lambda this equation is linear, so it is a plane, and any point lying on BOTH given planes makes each bracket zero and so satisfies it - hence it passes through their common line. The single free constant lambda is then chosen to make the plane satisfy one extra condition, for instance passing through a particular point, or being perpendicular to a given plane. For example, to find the plane through the intersection of x + y + z = 1 and 2x + 3y + 4z = 5 that passes through (1, 0, 0): write (x + y + z - 1) + lambda(2x + 3y + 4z - 5) = 0; substituting (1, 0, 0) gives (1 - 1) + lambda(2 - 5) = 0, so -3 lambda = 0, lambda = 0, giving x + y + z = 1 itself. Choosing a point not on the first plane yields a genuinely new plane.

35.10 WORKED NUMERICALS

Example 1. Reduce 3x - 6y + 2z - 14 = 0 to normal form and find the distance from the origin. Here sqrt(9 + 36 + 4) = 7; dividing and keeping the right side positive gives (3/7)x - (6/7)y + (2/7)z = 2. So the distance from the origin is p = 2 and the direction cosines of the normal are (3/7, -6/7, 2/7).

Example 2. Find the equation of the plane through (1, -2, 4) perpendicular to the line with direction (2, 3, -1). The normal is (2, 3, -1), so the plane is 2(x-1) + 3(y+2) - (z-4) = 0, i.e. 2x + 3y - z + 8 = 0.

Example 3. Find the angle between 2x - y + z = 4 and x + y + 2z = 3. Here n1 . n2 = (2)(1) + (-1)(1) + (1)(2) = 3, |n1| = sqrt(6), |n2| = sqrt(6), so cos theta = 3/6 = 1/2 and theta = 60 degrees.

Example 4. Find the distance of the point (2, -1, 3) from the plane 2x - 2y + z + 3 = 0. Substituting: |2(2) - 2(-1) + 3 + 3| / sqrt(4+4+1) = |4 + 2 + 3 + 3|/3 = 12/3 = 4 units.

SUMMARY

- General equation: Ax + By + Cz + D = 0, with normal vector n = (A, B, C); D = 0 means the plane passes through the origin.
- Normal form: lx + my + nz = p, where (l, m, n) are the direction cosines of the perpendicular from the origin and p (>0) is its length; obtained by dividing Ax+By+Cz+D=0 by sqrt(A^2+B^2+C^2).
- Plane through P(x1,y1,z1) with normal (A,B,C): A(x-x1)+B(y-y1)+C(z-z1)=0; in vectors r.n = a.n.
- Intercept form: x/a + y/b + z/c = 1, where a, b, c are the axis intercepts.
- Plane through three points: use the determinant of the three edge vectors, or the cross product of two edge vectors as the normal.
- Vector equation: r . n = d (with unit normal, r . n_hat = p).
- Angle between planes: cos theta = |n1 . n2|/(|n1||n2|). Parallel: A1/A2 = B1/B2 = C1/C2. Perpendicular: A1A2 + B1B2 + C1C2 = 0.
- Distance of a point: d = |A x1 + B y1 + C z1 + D|/sqrt(A^2+B^2+C^2); parallel-plane distance |D1-D2|/sqrt(A^2+B^2+C^2).
- Plane through the intersection of two planes: (A1x+B1y+C1z+D1) + lambda(A2x+B2y+C2z+D2) = 0, with lambda fixed by one more condition.

questions.question: Write the general equation of a plane and state what the coefficients of x, y and z represent. What does the plane pass through if D = 0 ?
questions.answer:
The general equation of a plane is

   Ax + By + Cz + D = 0

where A, B, C are not all zero. The coefficients of x, y and z, namely (A, B, C), are the components of the NORMAL VECTOR to the plane - a direction perpendicular to the surface. The constant D fixes the position of the plane. If D = 0, the point (0, 0, 0) satisfies the equation, so the plane PASSES THROUGH THE ORIGIN.
questions.explanation: General form + normal = (A,B,C); D = 0 means through origin.

questions.question: Reduce the plane 2x - 2y + z = 12 to normal form and hence write down the direction cosines of the normal and the distance of the plane from the origin.
questions.answer:
Here sqrt(A^2+B^2+C^2) = sqrt(4+4+1) = sqrt(9) = 3.
Divide 2x - 2y + z = 12 by 3:

   (2/3)x - (2/3)y + (1/3)z = 4

This is the normal form lx + my + nz = p.
Direction cosines of the normal: (2/3, -2/3, 1/3).
Distance of the plane from the origin: p = 4 units.

questions.question: Find the equation of the plane passing through the point (2, 3, -1) and having normal vector (4, 5, 6).
questions.answer:
Using the point-normal form A(x-x1)+B(y-y1)+C(z-z1)=0 with P(2,3,-1) and normal (4,5,6):

   4(x - 2) + 5(y - 3) + 6(z + 1) = 0

   4x - 8 + 5y - 15 + 6z + 6 = 0

   4x + 5y + 6z - 17 = 0.

So the required plane is 4x + 5y + 6z = 17.

questions.question: Find the intercepts made on the coordinate axes by the plane 2x + 3y + 4z = 12, and write its intercept form.
questions.answer:
Divide both sides by 12 to make the right side 1:

   2x/12 + 3y/12 + 4z/12 = 1

   x/6 + y/4 + z/3 = 1

Comparing with x/a + y/b + z/c = 1, the intercepts are a = 6 on the x-axis, b = 4 on the y-axis and c = 3 on the z-axis.

questions.question: Find the perpendicular distance of the point (2, -1, 3) from the plane 2x - 2y + z + 3 = 0.
Find the angle between the planes 2x - y + z = 4 and x + y + 2z = 3.
questions.answer:
The angle between the planes equals the angle between their normals n1 = (2,-1,1) and n2 = (1,1,2).

   n1 . n2 = (2)(1) + (-1)(1) + (1)(2) = 2 - 1 + 2 = 3

   |n1| = sqrt(4+1+1) = sqrt(6),  |n2| = sqrt(1+1+4) = sqrt(6)

   cos theta = |3| / (sqrt(6) sqrt(6)) = 3/6 = 1/2

Hence theta = 60 degrees.

questions.question: Reduce the plane 3x - 6y + 2z - 14 = 0 to normal form. Hence find (a) the direction cosines of the normal, (b) the perpendicular distance of the plane from the origin, and (c) the foot of the perpendicular from the origin.
questions.answer:
sqrt(A^2+B^2+C^2) = sqrt(9 + 36 + 4) = sqrt(49) = 7.
Write the equation as 3x - 6y + 2z = 14 and divide by 7:

   (3/7)x - (6/7)y + (2/7)z = 2

This is the normal form lx + my + nz = p.
(a) Direction cosines of the normal: (3/7, -6/7, 2/7).
(b) Perpendicular distance from the origin: p = 2 units.
(c) The foot of the perpendicular N lies at distance p along the unit normal from the origin: N = p(l, m, n) = 2(3/7, -6/7, 2/7) = (6/7, -12/7, 4/7).

questions.question: Find the equation of the plane passing through the three points (1, 1, 1), (1, 2, 3) and (2, -1, 1).
questions.explanation: Cross product gives normal (4,2,-1); plane 4x + 2y - z = 5.

questions.question: Find the equation of the plane passing through the line of intersection of the planes x + y + z = 6 and 2x + 3y + 4z = 5, and through the point (1, 1, 1).
questions.answer:
Any plane through the intersection line is

   (x + y + z - 6) + lambda(2x + 3y + 4z - 5) = 0.

It must pass through (1, 1, 1). Substitute:

   (1 + 1 + 1 - 6) + lambda(2 + 3 + 4 - 5) = 0
   (-3) + lambda(4) = 0
   lambda = 3/4.

Put lambda = 3/4 into the family:
   (x + y + z - 6) + (3/4)(2x + 3y + 4z - 5) = 0.
Multiply through by 4:
   4(x + y + z - 6) + 3(2x + 3y + 4z - 5) = 0
   4x + 4y + 4z - 24 + 6x + 9y + 12z - 15 = 0
   10x + 13y + 16z - 39 = 0.

So the required plane is 10x + 13y + 16z = 39. (Check (1,1,1): 10 + 13 + 16 = 39.)

questions.question: Explain the meaning of the normal form lx + my + nz = p of a plane. What do l, m, n and p stand for?
questions.answer: In the normal form lx + my + nz = p, the numbers l, m, n are the DIRECTION COSINES of the perpendicular drawn from the origin to the plane, so l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1. The number p is the LENGTH of that perpendicular, i.e. the perpendicular distance of the plane from the origin, and is taken positive. Thus the normal form displays both the orientation of the plane (through l, m, n) and its distance from the origin (through p).
questions.explanation: l,m,n = direction cosines of normal; p = distance from origin.

questions.question: Reduce the plane x + 2y + 2z = 9 to normal form and state the distance of the plane from the origin.
questions.answer:

   (1/3)x + (2/3)y + (2/3)z = 3

This is the normal form lx + my + nz = p with direction cosines (1/3, 2/3, 2/3) and p = 3. So the plane is at a distance of 3 units from the origin.

questions.question: Reduce -2x + y - 2z + 9 = 0 to normal form, taking care that the right-hand side is positive.

   (2/3)x - (1/3)y + (2/3)z = 3.

This is the normal form; the direction cosines of the normal are (2/3, -1/3, 2/3) and the distance from the origin is p = 3.
questions.explanation: Fix sign so RHS positive; divide by 3; p = 3.

questions.question: Find the equation of the plane passing through the point (3, -1, 2) and having normal vector (1, -2, 2).

   x - 3 - 2y - 2 + 2z - 4 = 0
   x - 2y + 2z - 9 = 0.

questions.question: Find the equation of the plane through the intersection of x + y + z = 6 and 2x + 3y + 4z = 5 that passes through the point (1, 1, 1).

   (1+1+1-6) + lambda(2+3+4-5) = 0
   (-3) + lambda(4) = 0  =>  lambda = 3/4.
Put lambda = 3/4 and multiply by 4:
   4(x+y+z-6) + 3(2x+3y+4z-5) = 0
   4x+4y+4z-24 + 6x+9y+12z-15 = 0
   10x + 13y + 16z - 39 = 0.

questions.question: A plane passes through the point (2, 3, -1) and is perpendicular to the line joining (1, 0, 2) and (3, 4, 0). Find its equation and hence the perpendicular distance of the origin from it.

Use the point-normal form through (2,3,-1) with normal (1,2,-1):
   1(x - 2) + 2(y - 3) - 1(z + 1) = 0
   x + 2y - z - 9 = 0.
So the plane is x + 2y - z = 9.
Distance of the origin (0,0,0):
   d = |0 + 0 - 0 - 9|/sqrt(1+4+1) = 9/sqrt(6) = 9/sqrt(6) = (9 sqrt(6))/6 = (3 sqrt(6))/2, about 3.67 units.

questions.question: Derive the vector equation of a plane r . n = d starting from a point a on the plane and a normal n. Then use it to find the plane through a = i + j + k with normal n = 2i - j + 2k, and write the Cartesian form.
questions.answer:
Derivation: Let a be the position vector of a fixed point A on the plane and n a normal vector. If R (position vector r) is any point of the plane, then the vector AR = r - a lies IN the plane, and so is perpendicular to the normal n. Perpendicularity means their dot product is zero:
   (r - a) . n = 0
   r . n - a . n = 0
   r . n = a . n.
Writing d = a . n (a constant), the vector equation is r . n = d.

Application: a = i + j + k, n = 2i - j + 2k.
   d = a . n = (1)(2) + (1)(-1) + (1)(2) = 2 - 1 + 2 = 3.
So r . (2i - j + 2k) = 3.
With r = x i + y j + z k, the Cartesian form is 2x - y + 2z = 3.

   n1 . n2 = 2 - 1 + 2 = 3; |n1| = sqrt(6), |n2| = sqrt(6).
   cos theta = 3/6 = 1/2, so theta = 60 degrees.

A plane perpendicular to both given planes has a normal perpendicular to both n1 and n2, i.e. along n1 x n2:
   n1 x n2:
     i: (-1)(2) - (1)(1) = -3
     j: -[(2)(2) - (1)(1)] = -3
     k: (2)(1) - (-1)(1) = 3
   So the normal is (-3, -3, 3), or simplified (1, 1, -1).
Since the plane passes through the origin, D = 0:
   x + y - z = 0.
That is the required plane.
questions.explanation: theta = 60 degrees; cross product normal (1,1,-1); plane x + y - z = 0.

questions.question: The point P is (3, -2, 1). (a) Find the perpendicular distance of P from the plane 2x - 2y + z + 3 = 0. (b) Find the distance of the origin from the same plane. (c) Find the distance between this plane and the parallel plane 2x - 2y + z - 6 = 0.
Find the equation of the plane through the line of intersection of the planes x + y + z = 1 and 2x + 3y + 4z = 5 which is perpendicular to the plane x - y + z = 0.
questions.answer:
Family through the intersection:
   (x + y + z - 1) + lambda(2x + 3y + 4z - 5) = 0
   (1 + 2 lambda)x + (1 + 3 lambda)y + (1 + 4 lambda)z - (1 + 5 lambda) = 0.
Its normal is N = (1 + 2 lambda, 1 + 3 lambda, 1 + 4 lambda).
This plane is perpendicular to x - y + z = 0, whose normal is (1, -1, 1). Perpendicular planes have normals with zero dot product:
   (1)(1 + 2 lambda) + (-1)(1 + 3 lambda) + (1)(1 + 4 lambda) = 0
   1 + 2 lambda - 1 - 3 lambda + 1 + 4 lambda = 0
   1 + 3 lambda = 0  =>  lambda = -1/3.
Substitute lambda = -1/3 and multiply through by 3:
   3(x + y + z - 1) - (2x + 3y + 4z - 5) = 0
   3x + 3y + 3z - 3 - 2x - 3y - 4z + 5 = 0
   x - z + 2 = 0.
So the required plane is x - z + 2 = 0.
questions.explanation: Family normal dotted with (1,-1,1)=0 gives lambda=-1/3; plane x - z + 2 = 0.

questions.question: Show that the planes 2x - 2y + 4z + 5 = 0 and 3x - 3y + 6z - 1 = 0 are parallel, and find the distance between them.
questions.answer:
Normals: n1 = (2,-2,4) and n2 = (3,-3,6). Since 3/2 = -3/-2 = 6/4 = 3/2, the normals are proportional, so the planes are PARALLEL.
To find the distance, make the normals identical. Divide the first by 2: x - y + 2z + 5/2 = 0. Divide the second by 3: x - y + 2z - 1/3 = 0.
Now use |D1 - D2|/sqrt(A^2+B^2+C^2) with D1 = 5/2, D2 = -1/3, and sqrt(1+1+4) = sqrt(6):
   |5/2 - (-1/3)| = |15/6 + 2/6| = 17/6.
   Distance = (17/6)/sqrt(6) = 17/(6 sqrt(6)) = (17 sqrt(6))/36, about 1.16 units.
questions.explanation: Proportional normals => parallel; scale to common normal; distance 17/(6 sqrt(6)).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Every plane in space is represented by a first-degree equation Ax + By + Cz + D = 0, where A, B, C are not all zero. The triple (A, B, C) is the normal vector, which fixes the tilt of the plane, while D fixes its position. When D = 0 the plane passes through the origin. The coordinate planes are x = 0, y = 0 and z = 0.
(a) Write the normal vector of the plane 3x - 4y + z - 7 = 0.
(b) Does this plane pass through the origin? Why?
(c) Which coordinate plane does z = 0 represent?
(d) What does the constant D control in the equation?
questions.answer:
(a) The normal vector is (3, -4, 1), the coefficients of x, y and z.
(b) No. Substituting the origin gives 3(0) - 4(0) + 0 - 7 = -7, which is not zero; equivalently D = -7 is non-zero, so the plane does not pass through the origin.
(c) z = 0 represents the xy-plane.
(d) D fixes the POSITION of the plane (how far it is shifted from the origin); with the same (A,B,C) different values of D give parallel planes.
questions.explanation: Normal (3,-4,1); not through origin; z=0 is xy-plane; D fixes position.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A plane can be reduced to normal form lx + my + nz = p by dividing Ax + By + Cz + D = 0 by sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + C^2) and arranging the sign so the right side is positive. Then (l, m, n) are the direction cosines of the normal and p is the perpendicular distance of the plane from the origin. Consider the plane 2x - 2y + z = 12.
(a) Find sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + C^2).
(b) Write the normal form.
(c) State the direction cosines of the normal.
(d) State the distance of the plane from the origin.
questions.answer:
(a) sqrt(A^2+B^2+C^2) = sqrt(4 + 4 + 1) = sqrt(9) = 3.
(b) Divide by 3: (2/3)x - (2/3)y + (1/3)z = 4. This is the normal form.
(c) Direction cosines of the normal: (2/3, -2/3, 1/3).
(d) The distance from the origin is p = 4 units.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A plane is fixed by one point on it and a direction normal to it. If P(x1,y1,z1) lies on the plane and (A,B,C) is normal, then A(x-x1)+B(y-y1)+C(z-z1)=0. In vectors this is r . n = a . n. Consider the point (2, 3, -1) and normal (4, 5, 6).
(a) Write the point-normal equation.
(b) Simplify it to general form.
(c) Write its vector equation r . n = d, giving d.
(d) Verify that (2, 3, -1) lies on the plane.

Read the passage and answer the questions.
When a plane meets the axes at (a,0,0), (0,b,0) and (0,0,c), its equation is the intercept form x/a + y/b + z/c = 1. To read off the intercepts from a general equation, write the constant on the right and divide through. Consider 2x + 3y + 4z = 12.
(a) Write the plane in intercept form.
(b) State the x, y and z intercepts.
(c) What is the equation of a plane with intercepts 3, 3, 3?
(d) Why does a plane parallel to the x-axis have no x term?
questions.answer:
(a) Divide by 12: x/6 + y/4 + z/3 = 1.
(b) x-intercept 6, y-intercept 4, z-intercept 3.
(c) x/3 + y/3 + z/3 = 1, i.e. x + y + z = 3.
(d) A plane parallel to the x-axis never meets it, so its x-intercept is infinite; in the equation x/a -> 0, which removes the x term.
questions.explanation: x/6+y/4+z/3=1; intercepts 6,4,3; x+y+z=3; parallel => no x term.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The vector equation of a plane is r . n = d, where n is a normal vector, r is the position vector of a point on the plane, and d = a . n for a fixed point a. With a unit normal it becomes r . n_hat = p, the perpendicular distance p from the origin. Consider a = 2i + 3j - k and n = i + 2j + 2k.
(a) Compute d = a . n.
(b) Write the vector equation.
(c) Write the Cartesian equation.
(d) Find the unit normal n_hat.

Read the passage and answer the questions.
The angle between two planes equals the angle between their normals: cos theta = |n1 . n2|/(|n1||n2|). The planes are parallel if their normals are proportional and perpendicular if n1 . n2 = 0. Consider the planes x + 2y + 2z = 5 and 2x - y + 2z = 3.
(a) Write the two normals.
(b) Compute n1 . n2.
(c) Find cos theta.
(d) Are these planes parallel, perpendicular or neither?
questions.answer:
(a) n1 = (1, 2, 2) and n2 = (2, -1, 2).
(b) n1 . n2 = (1)(2) + (2)(-1) + (2)(2) = 2 - 2 + 4 = 4.
(c) |n1| = sqrt(1+4+4) = 3, |n2| = sqrt(4+1+4) = 3; cos theta = |4|/(3 x 3) = 4/9.
(d) Neither: n1 . n2 = 4 is not zero (not perpendicular) and the normals are not proportional (not parallel). The angle is cos^-1(4/9), about 63.6 degrees.
questions.explanation: Normals (1,2,2),(2,-1,2); dot=4; cos=4/9; neither parallel nor perpendicular.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The perpendicular distance of P(x1,y1,z1) from Ax+By+Cz+D=0 is |Ax1+By1+Cz1+D|/sqrt(A^2+B^2+C^2). The distance between parallel planes with the same normal is |D1-D2|/sqrt(A^2+B^2+C^2). Consider the plane 2x - 2y + z + 3 = 0.
(a) Find the distance of (2, -1, 3) from it.
(b) Find the distance of the origin from it.
(c) Find the distance to the parallel plane 2x - 2y + z - 9 = 0.
(d) What is the denominator common to all these calculations?
questions.answer:
(a) |2(2) - 2(-1) + 1(3) + 3|/sqrt(4+4+1) = |4 + 2 + 3 + 3|/3 = 12/3 = 4 units.
(b) |2(0) - 2(0) + 0 + 3|/3 = 3/3 = 1 unit.
(c) Parallel planes: D1 = 3, D2 = -9; distance = |3 - (-9)|/3 = 12/3 = 4 units.
(d) The common denominator is sqrt(A^2+B^2+C^2) = sqrt(4+4+1) = 3, the length of the normal.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Two non-parallel planes meet in a line, and every plane through that line is (P1) + lambda(P2) = 0, where lambda is a parameter fixed by one extra condition. Consider P1: x + y + z - 6 = 0 and P2: 2x + 3y + 4z - 5 = 0.
(a) Write the general member of the family.
(b) Find lambda so that the plane passes through (1, 1, 1).
(c) Write the resulting plane.
(d) Explain why every member of the family passes through the intersection line.
questions.answer:
(a) (x + y + z - 6) + lambda(2x + 3y + 4z - 5) = 0.
(b) Substitute (1,1,1): (1+1+1-6) + lambda(2+3+4-5) = -3 + 4 lambda = 0, so lambda = 3/4.
(c) Multiply by 4: 4(x+y+z-6) + 3(2x+3y+4z-5) = 0 => 10x + 13y + 16z - 39 = 0, i.e. 10x + 13y + 16z = 39.
(d) Any point on both P1 and P2 makes each bracket zero, so the whole expression is 0 + lambda(0) = 0 for every lambda; hence every member contains the common line of intersection.
questions.explanation: Family form; lambda=3/4; plane 10x+13y+16z=39; both brackets vanish on the line.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
When reducing a plane to normal form, the right-hand side p must be positive because it is a distance. If dividing by sqrt(A^2+B^2+C^2) leaves a negative right side, multiply the whole equation by -1 first. Consider -3x + 4y - 12z + 26 = 0.
(a) Rearrange so the constant is on the right and make it positive.
(b) Find sqrt(A^2+B^2+C^2).
(c) Write the normal form.
(d) State the distance from the origin.
questions.answer:
(a) -3x + 4y - 12z = -26; multiply by -1: 3x - 4y + 12z = 26.
(b) sqrt(9 + 16 + 144) = sqrt(169) = 13.
(c) Divide by 13: (3/13)x - (4/13)y + (12/13)z = 2.
(d) The distance from the origin is p = 2 units.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Parallelism and perpendicularity of planes are read from their normals. Planes are parallel when A1/A2 = B1/B2 = C1/C2 and perpendicular when A1A2 + B1B2 + C1C2 = 0. Consider three planes: P: x + 2y - z = 3, Q: 2x + 4y - 2z = 7, R: 2x - y + 0z = 4.
(a) Are P and Q parallel? Justify.
(b) Are P and R perpendicular? Justify.
(c) Give the normal of each of P and R.
(d) Can two distinct parallel planes ever intersect?
questions.answer:
(a) Yes. Normals are (1,2,-1) and (2,4,-2); since 2/1 = 4/2 = -2/-1 = 2, they are proportional, so P and Q are parallel.
(b) Yes. P has normal (1,2,-1) and R has normal (2,-1,0); their dot product is (1)(2) + (2)(-1) + (-1)(0) = 2 - 2 + 0 = 0, so P and R are perpendicular.
(c) Normal of P is (1, 2, -1); normal of R is (2, -1, 0).
(d) No. Distinct parallel planes never meet; they stay a constant distance apart.
questions.explanation: P||Q (ratio 2); P perp R (dot 0); normals (1,2,-1),(2,-1,0); parallel never meet.
